Accenture — Skills to Succeed Academy
Programme Summary
The Accenture Skills to Succeed Academy is a comprehensive online learning programme covering 114 modules across three pillars: Employability (resume writing, CAR technique, interview skills), Professional Growth (soft skills, digital communication, and CPD), and Digital Proficiency (Coding, Data, AI, and Technology). Key frameworks include the CAR (Context, Action, Result) interview technique, the four-stage CPD cycle (Plan, Do, Check, Act), and the POP (Pick Out the Positives) method for professional resilience.
🎯
Accenture · Skills to Succeed Academy
Skills to Succeed — Employability
Choose a Career · Getting a Job · Success in Work
▾
Description
This cluster teaches how to transition from academic life to professional employment. It covers identifying personal strengths, tailoring a resume for specific roles, understanding the selection process, and communicating competency using the CAR (Context, Action, Result) technique. Students also learned how to build a professional online presence, master virtual interviews, and use networking tools like LinkedIn and JobStreet.
Key Learnings
The CAR Technique — structuring interview answers around Context, Action, and Result to quantify impact rather than just list duties.
Resume tailoring — every application requires a role-specific resume that removes irrelevant skills and highlights applicable experience.
Virtual interview skills — maintaining professionalism and clear communication in remote hiring scenarios.
What · So What · Now What
What
Having direction while staying adaptable is the most critical professional skill in a fast-changing digital economy.
So What
This bridges the gap between IT knowledge and workplace survival — knowing how to communicate a skill's value is just as important as having the skill.
Now What
Apply the Tailored Resume strategy to every internship application and adopt the POP method to maintain a professional attitude during challenging projects.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
CAR and SuperCAR mastery for structured interview storytelling.
Weaknesses
Being at the Starting Out phase with limited work experience.
Opportunities
Virtual workplace and remote job opportunities globally.
Threats
AI automation replacing repetitive or entry-level task roles.
💻
Accenture · Skills to Succeed Academy
Skills to Succeed — Technology
Exploring Coding · Discovering Data · Technology at Work
▾
Description
This cluster introduced technical foundations of the modern digital economy — 12 coding languages (Python, JavaScript, and more), web and app development basics, data interpretation, cloud computing, AI, and blockchain. Students explored how digitalization transforms workplaces and how to work efficiently in virtual environments.
Key Learnings
Digitalization fundamentally changes how organizations operate, communicate, and deliver value — not just the tools they use.
Python and JavaScript are foundational for both data science and web/app development, making them high-priority skills.
Data is growing to 163 zettabytes by 2025 — data literacy is now an essential skill across all industries.
What · So What · Now What
What
Seeing the timeline from radio (1895) to smartphone (2007) to 4D printing highlighted that adaptability is the most valuable career skill.
So What
Technical skills must be paired with the ability to communicate their value — coding ability alone does not guarantee career success.
Now What
Stay technologically current by following the UT5 guide: subscribe to tech newsletters, follow industry influencers, and continuously practice coding.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Foundational knowledge in 12 coding languages and 5 data chart types.
Weaknesses
Theoretical exposure without deep hands-on project experience.
Opportunities
AI integration in retail, finance, gaming, and smart home sectors.
Threats
Rapid tech obsolescence — tools like Perl replaced by newer stacks.
🌱
Accenture · Skills to Succeed Academy
Lifelong Learning
Growth Mindset · CPD Cycle · Learning Quotient
▾
Description
This module explores sustained self-improvement by distinguishing a fixed mindset (abilities are static) from a growth mindset (abilities grow through effort). It teaches the four-stage CPD cycle (Plan, Do, Check, Act) and reframes challenges, mistakes, and feedback as essential catalysts for growth.
Key Learnings
People with a growth mindset view effort as the path to mastery — unlike a fixed mindset that avoids challenges to protect self-image.
The CPD Cycle provides a structured approach to professional development that prevents skill stagnation.
Challenges, failure, and feedback are the primary mechanisms through which genuine learning occurs.
What · So What · Now What
What
Believing in my ability to improve is itself the first step — mindset precedes action.
So What
Failure is a necessary feedback mechanism, not a measure of permanent ability — this reframing changes how I approach setbacks.
Now What
Practice lifelong learning by being open to new skills, actively seeking feedback, and applying the growth mindset to every challenge in school and work.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Internalized CPD cycle for structured career development.
Weaknesses
Self-paced learning requires strong personal discipline.
Opportunities
Continuously upgrade skills as technology evolves.
Threats
Overreliance on comfort zones preventing skill growth.
🧩
Accenture · Skills to Succeed Academy
Solving Problems
Problem Definition · Brainstorming · Decision Making
▾
Description
This module presents problem-solving as a structured, learnable process — not an innate talent. It covers root causes of workplace problems (poor communication, role overload) and introduces a step-by-step approach: define the problem clearly, brainstorm solutions, evaluate options using Pros/Cons and Good-Better-Best frameworks, and take measurable action.
Key Learnings
Problems often have multiple root causes — jumping to solutions without understanding the cause leads to recurring issues.
The 'Pros and Cons' and 'Good, Better, Best?' frameworks help evaluate solutions objectively rather than emotionally.
Verifying assumptions before acting prevents wasted effort on solutions built on false premises.
What · So What · Now What
What
Learning that every problem has a solution when approached calmly and methodically — being calm and organized is key.
So What
Instead of feeling stuck, I now know to pause, define the real problem, and systematically work toward a solution.
Now What
Apply problem-solving steps when facing academic and personal challenges, practicing identifying the core issue before jumping to solutions.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Structured frameworks for tackling both simple and complex problems.
Weaknesses
Tendency to feel overwhelmed before methodically breaking down the problem.
Opportunities
Apply problem-solving skills to academic projects and internship tasks.
Threats
Panic and impulsive decision-making under time pressure.
💡
Accenture · Skills to Succeed Academy
Thinking Critically
Critical Analysis · Questioning · Information Literacy
▾
Description
This module defines critical thinking as analyzing and evaluating information using reason rather than emotion. It outlines five steps (formulating questions, gathering information, applying evidence, considering implications, evaluating perspectives) and the 5Ws and 1H framework for deep inquiry.
Key Learnings
Critical thinking requires intellectual humility — being willing to revise beliefs when evidence contradicts them.
The 'Is This Real or Fake?' module taught how to evaluate information sources for credibility, relevance, and bias.
Being analytical does not mean being negative — it means asking the right questions to arrive at well-supported conclusions.
What · So What · Now What
What
Critical thinking is not about doubting everything — it is about asking the right questions to understand information more deeply and accurately.
So What
This skill is directly applicable to every IT research task, helping evaluate sources, challenge assumptions, and make better-informed decisions.
Now What
Practice by asking questions before accepting information, checking facts across multiple sources, and considering alternative perspectives.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Ability to analyze information carefully and avoid misinformation.
Weaknesses
Natural tendency to accept information at face value without questioning.
Opportunities
Improved research quality and academic writing through critical analysis.
Threats
Misinformation and fake news require constant vigilance.
💜
Accenture · Skills to Succeed Academy
Emotional Intelligence
Self-Regulation · Active Listening · Conflict Management
▾
Description
This module covers emotional intelligence (EI) as the ability to recognize, understand, and manage emotions — both one's own and others'. It teaches the S.T.O.P.P. method (Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Pull back, Practise) for emotional regulation, active listening techniques, audience awareness, and constructive workplace conflict management.
Key Learnings
The S.T.O.P.P. method provides a pause-and-reflect technique before reacting emotionally to stressful situations.
Active listening requires full attention, acknowledgment, and thoughtful response — not just waiting for a turn to speak.
Knowing your audience means adapting communication style to the listener's background, emotional state, and expectations.
What · So What · Now What
What
Having emotions is normal — what defines professionalism is how we choose to respond, not whether we feel them.
So What
EI is as important as technical knowledge. Understanding myself and managing interactions will directly affect my effectiveness in any team.
Now What
Practice staying calm during difficult situations, listening actively before responding, and applying S.T.O.P.P. when experiencing emotional stress.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Understanding the S.T.O.P.P. method for emotional regulation in high-pressure situations.
Weaknesses
Emotional responses are habitual — changing them requires consistent conscious practice.
Opportunities
EI improves teamwork, leadership, and professional relationships.
Threats
Unmanaged stress or conflict escalation in academic group projects.
🤖
Accenture · Skills to Succeed Academy
Gen AI Fundamentals
Generative AI · Prompting · Responsible Use
▾
Description
This module introduces Generative AI as technology that creates content by learning patterns from datasets. It covers effective prompt writing, AI limitations (hallucinations, bias), personal data protection, and responsible use principles. The module emphasizes AI as a support tool — not a replacement for human judgment.
Key Learnings
Prompt engineering is critical — the quality of AI output is directly determined by the clarity and specificity of the input.
Gen AI can produce plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information (hallucinations), making independent fact-checking essential.
Responsible AI use requires protecting personal data, verifying outputs, and understanding ethical implications of AI-generated content.
What · So What · Now What
What
AI is not infallible — I must not outsource my thinking to it but use it as a sophisticated starting point that I verify and refine.
So What
I need to be more deliberate when using AI tools, treating outputs as drafts requiring my own evaluation rather than finished answers.
Now What
Use Generative AI to help organize ideas and study, always double-check outputs, write better prompts, and apply it responsibly in academic work.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Understanding AI limitations helps use it more critically and effectively.
Weaknesses
AI's tendency to produce confident-sounding errors requires constant vigilance.
Opportunities
Use Gen AI as a study and research support tool to boost productivity.
Threats
AI misinformation or misuse can affect academic and professional integrity.

Cisco Networking Academy
Cyber Threat Management
Mar 25, 2026 · DICT-ITU DTC Initiative · Instructor: Pollyne Villanueva
▾
Description
This course covered the full lifecycle of organizational cybersecurity management — from establishing ethical conduct policies to executing disaster recovery after a breach. Students used network diagnostic tools (ipconfig, netstat) and packet sniffers (Wireshark) to monitor traffic and identify vulnerabilities. The course covered how to interpret threat intelligence reports, build risk management plans, and ensure business continuity. A core lesson: security is both technical and managerial — effective cyber defense requires governance, legal compliance, and human awareness alongside technical tools.
Key Learnings
Visibility is Security — you cannot protect what you cannot see; Wireshark and netstat confirm that encrypted protocols (SSH) are used over insecure ones (Telnet).
Legal compliance as protection — HIPAA and PCI-DSS are not bureaucratic obstacles but critical safeguards for sensitive data in healthcare and finance.
Risk can never be fully eliminated — only managed through Avoidance, Mitigation, Transfer, or Acceptance, each requiring a Disaster Recovery Plan.
What · So What · Now What
What
Seeing how easily unencrypted Telnet data can be captured in plain text made abstract threats feel immediate and real.
So What
Cybersecurity is multi-layered — it requires policy, ethics, physical infrastructure, and human behavior management, not just technical tools.
Now What
Default to encrypted protocols, conduct regular vulnerability assessments, and create Disaster Recovery Plans for every organization I work with.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Diagnostic toolset (Packet Tracer, Wireshark) for deep network visibility and compliance focus (HIPAA/PCI-DSS).
Weaknesses
Complexity of maintaining compliance in a changing regulatory landscape; human error as a persistent vulnerability.
Opportunities
AI/ML integration for vulnerability scan data; OSINT for real-time threat monitoring.
Threats
Advanced persistent threats (APTs) and zero-day exploits targeting unpatched systems.

Cisco Networking Academy
Endpoint Security
Apr 15, 2026 · Cisco Networking Academy · Director: Lynn Bloomer
▾
Description
This course explored endpoint security through the McCumber Cube — a three-dimensional framework evaluating security across Data States (Storage, Transmission, Processing), Principles (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability), and Safeguard Types (Technology, Policy, Human Factors). Hands-on labs covered MD5/SHA-256 hashing, AES-256-CBC encryption with OpenSSL, and Linux system hardening using Lynis. Social engineering attacks (phishing, pretexting, ransomware) were analyzed to illustrate that the human element is consistently the weakest link.
Key Learnings
The CIA Triad is multi-dimensional — protecting data requires different controls depending on whether it is stored, in transit, or being processed.
Hashing vs. Encryption — hashing (MD5/SHA-256) verifies data integrity while encryption (AES-256) ensures confidentiality for authorized users only.
Proactive system hardening with Lynis generates a prioritized list of vulnerabilities to address before attackers can exploit them.
What · So What · Now What
What
Even with AES-256 encryption, a single phishing email or tailgating incident can lead to total system compromise — technical security is only as strong as its human layer.
So What
Security must be viewed as a 'Cube' where every dimension is secured simultaneously. Addressing only encryption while neglecting user education creates exploitable gaps.
Now What
Apply a hardening mindset to every system managed: deploy firewalls, focus on user education, conduct regular integrity checks, and use behavioral analysis for layered defense.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
McCumber Cube framework addresses security across three dimensions simultaneously.
Weaknesses
Human psychology remains the most significant vulnerability — phishing bypasses even strong technical controls.
Opportunities
Automation of security audits using PowerShell and Linux scripts reduces human error.
Threats
SQL injection and polymorphic malware pose persistent threats to web applications.
🌐
Cisco Networking Academy
Digital Safety & Security Awareness
Apr 15, 2026 · DICT-ITU DTC Initiative · Instructor: Roma Herminigildo
▾
Description
This self-paced modular course cultivated a proactive mindset toward digital hygiene. Modules covered device hardening, privacy settings, phishing psychology, digital footprint permanence, and the Dark Web. The curriculum emphasized that digital security is deeply connected to human behavior, media literacy, and responsible online conduct. Modern attacks exploit urgency and emotion to bypass rational judgment — making critical thinking a security skill.
Key Learnings
Digital footprints are permanent — every online action creates a searchable trail, making privacy settings a proactive first line of defense.
Phishing and social engineering attacks exploit urgency and emotion to override technical security — critical thinking is itself a security tool.
Holistic digital security requires combining strong passwords, regular updates, critical information literacy, and safe browsing habits.
What · So What · Now What
What
Learning how easily misinformation and threats spread online highlighted how much of our security depends on personal awareness — not just software.
So What
Daily internet use requires safer, more responsible decisions across all digital platforms — awareness is the first layer of protection.
Now What
Practice safe browsing, verify information before sharing, be cautious with unknown links, and stay informed about evolving digital safety practices.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Comprehensive coverage of both technical and behavioral dimensions of digital safety.
Weaknesses
Self-paced format offers no live instructor for immediate clarification of complex topics.
Opportunities
Skills directly applicable to academic work, future internships, and personal online safety.
Threats
Rapid threat evolution and technology changes may make specific techniques outdated quickly.

Cisco Networking Academy
Introduction to Data Science
Apr 15, 2026 · Cisco Networking Academy · Director: Lynn Bloomer
▾
Description
This course introduced the fundamentals of data science — extracting meaningful insights from raw data to support decision-making. Modules covered the data pipeline (collection, cleaning, analysis, visualization, interpretation), machine learning concepts, and real-world applications in business and healthcare. The course emphasized that data's value lies not in its volume but in the quality of insights derived from it.
Key Learnings
Data-driven decision-making replaces assumption-based thinking with evidence-based analysis, leading to better outcomes across all organizational functions.
Data analysis reveals hidden patterns and correlations not apparent through casual observation — these insights solve problems and drive innovation.
Data science skills are in high demand across virtually all industries, making data literacy a high-value differentiator in the job market.
What · So What · Now What
What
Learning how data influences real-world decisions — in healthcare, business forecasting, and technology — made data science immediately relevant rather than theoretical.
So What
This encourages evidence-based thinking rather than assumptions. Using data to validate decisions leads to better and more defensible outcomes in IT projects.
Now What
Develop data analysis skills by learning tools like Python (pandas, matplotlib) and practice data interpretation to prepare for internship and career opportunities.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Well-structured curriculum covering the full data science pipeline from collection to interpretation.
Weaknesses
Largely theoretical with limited access to large real-world datasets for hands-on practice.
Opportunities
Data skills directly applicable to IT internships, research projects, and future career roles.
Threats
Rapidly changing industry tools require constant learning to stay current.

De La Salle Lipa
DevRoutes: Learning How to Learn with Roadmaps
Jan 29, 2026 · MB Auditorium, De La Salle Lipa · Organizer: JPCS De La Salle Chapter · Speaker: Condeilamor Gantalao
▾
Description
The DevRoutes seminar, organized by the Junior Philippine Computer Society (JPCS) De La Salle Chapter, focused on career path planning for IT students. Speaker Condeilamor Gantalao shared his personal career journey — including pivots, decisions, and risks — to illustrate that professional success rarely follows a linear trajectory. The seminar emphasized that while a clear career roadmap provides direction, adaptability and willingness to seize unexpected opportunities are equally important. Students were encouraged to start mapping professional goals early, identify their strengths, and take calculated risks to accelerate growth.
Key Learnings
A personal career roadmap serves as a directional guide, not a rigid prescription — having a plan while remaining flexible is the professional ideal.
Real career journeys involve unexpected detours, and these deviations often lead to growth opportunities that a rigid plan would have missed.
Proactively seeking growth — by asking 'Can I do more?' and pursuing the answer — is the distinguishing mindset of high-performing professionals.
What · So What · Now What
What
The speaker's emphasis on creating a roadmap while accepting that success is not a straight path resonated strongly — it made the discussion realistic and personally applicable.
So What
Having direction is important, but flexibility is equally necessary. A career roadmap is a guide that should be revisited and revised as new opportunities and challenges emerge.
Now What
Start creating a personal career roadmap by identifying goals, strengths, and areas for improvement; remain open to different paths; take calculated risks when growth opportunities arise.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Real-life career journey shared made the content relatable and genuinely inspiring.
Weaknesses
Focused primarily on personal experience — may not cover all possible IT career paths.
Opportunities
Serves as a starting point for career planning; motivates early internship and skill development.
Threats
Students may become discouraged if plans don't unfold as expected and fail to adapt.

De La Salle Lipa
Innovative Research Horizons
Feb 3, 2026 · CBEAM Function Hall, De La Salle Lipa · Organizer: DLSL ACES & IECEP-DLSL SC · Speaker: Engr. Aisa Mijeno-Labastilla
▾
Description
The Innovative Research Horizons seminar, organized by DLSL ACES and IECEP-DLSL SC, introduced students to AI's transformative role in modern research. Speaker Engr. Aisa Mijeno-Labastilla explained how AI, machine learning, and deep learning are used to process large research datasets, identify patterns, and accelerate scientific discovery. The seminar presented a balanced view: AI offers extraordinary opportunities for research efficiency, but also introduces risks including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, and misuse potential. Central argument: AI is a tool — its value and ethical implications depend entirely on the human decision-making that directs it.
Key Learnings
AI offers research-accelerating opportunities such as faster pattern recognition, large-scale data analysis, and improved decision support across disciplines.
AI carries significant challenges including algorithmic bias, factual errors, and misuse risk — responsible implementation requires human oversight at every stage.
AI cannot replicate human intelligence — it lacks feelings, creative intuition, and moral reasoning, making it an augmentation tool, not a replacement.
What · So What · Now What
What
The realization that AI is powerful but fundamentally limited — it cannot think, feel, or create independently, and its outputs depend entirely on the quality of human direction.
So What
AI should be viewed as a sophisticated tool, not a replacement for human judgment. Human skills — critical thinking, creativity, and ethical reasoning — remain irreplaceable.
Now What
Use AI responsibly as a support tool in learning and research; develop stronger prompting and critical evaluation skills; stay mindful of ethical issues and regulatory developments.
SWOT Analysis
Strengths
Balanced presentation of both AI opportunities and limitations gave a realistic and nuanced perspective.
Weaknesses
Some advanced topics on AI bias and misuse may require deeper follow-up study to fully understand.
Opportunities
AI tools can support research, data analysis, and academic learning more efficiently.
Threats
Over-reliance on AI may weaken critical thinking; AI errors could compromise research integrity.
